translations.text: Every Christian should rightly know both his Pater noster and his Creed. With the Pater noster he should pray, and with the Creed he should strengthen his faith.
We have spoken about the Pater noster; now we will tell you the faith that is set out in the Creed, just as the wise Augustine explained it concerning the Holy Trinity.
There is one Creator of all things, visible and invisible; and we must believe in him, because he is true God and alone Almighty, who never began and never had a beginning;
but he himself is the beginning, and he gave to all creatures a beginning and origin, so that they might exist, and so that they had their own nature, just as it pleased the divine ordering.
He made angels, which are spirits and have no body. He created men with spirit and with body. He created cattle and wild beasts, fish and birds in flesh, without a soul.
To men he gave an upright walk; he let the cattle go bent over. To men he gave bread for food, and to the cattle grass.
Now, brothers, you can understand, if you will, that there are two things: one is the Creator, the other is creation.
He is the Creator who created and made all things out of nothing. Creation is what the true Creator created.
That is, first the heavens, and the angels who dwell in the heavens, and then this earth with all those who live on it, and the sea with all those that swim in it.
Now all these things are named with one name: creation. They were not always in existence, but God created them. The created things are many.
One is the Creator who created them all; he alone is Almighty God. He always was, and he will always be, continuing in himself and through himself.
If he had begun and had a beginning, then without doubt he could not be Almighty God; truly, the creature that began and is created has no divinity;
therefore every substance that is not God is creation, and whatever is not creation is God.
This God exists undivided in Trinity, and in the unity of one Godhead. Truly, the Father is one, the Son is another, the Holy Spirit is another;
but nevertheless, of the three there is one Godhead, and equal glory, and co-eternal majesty.
the Father is Almighty God, the Son is Almighty God, the Holy Spirit is Almighty God; but nevertheless they are not three Almighty Gods, but one Almighty God.
They are three in persons and in names, and one in Godhead. Three, because the Father is always Father, and the Son is always Son, and the Holy Spirit is always Holy Spirit;
and none of them ever changes from what he is. Now you have heard about the Holy Trinity; you must also hear about the true Unity.
Truly the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one Godhead, and one nature, and one work.
The Father did not make and does not make anything without the Son, or without the Holy Spirit.
None of them makes anything without the others; rather, they all have one work, and one counsel, and one will.
The Father always was, and the Son always was, and the Holy Spirit always was, one Almighty God. He is the Father who is neither born nor created by any other.
He is called Father because he has a Son, whom he begot from himself, without any mother. The Father is God from no God. The Son is God from God the Father.
The Holy Spirit is God proceeding from the Father and from the Son. These words are briefly said, and you need us to reveal them to you more clearly.
What is the Father? The Almighty Creator, neither made nor born; rather, he himself begot a Child co-eternal with himself.
What is the Son? He is the Father's Wisdom, and his Word, and his Power, through whom the Father created and ordered all things.
The Son is not made or created, but he is begotten. He is begotten, and nevertheless he is as old as his Father and co-eternal with him.
It is not with his birth as it is with our birth. When a man begets a son and his child is born, the father is greater and the son is lesser.
Why so? Because when the son grows, the father grows old. Among men you will not find a father and son who are equal.
But I will give you an example, so that you may better understand God's begetting. Fire begets brightness from itself, and the brightness is just as old as the fire.
The fire is not from the brightness, but the brightness is from the fire. The fire begets the brightness, but it is never without the brightness.
Now you hear that the brightness is just as old as the fire from which it comes; grant now, therefore, that God could beget a Child just as old,
Now you have heard that the Son is from the Father without any beginning, because he is the Father's Wisdom, and he was always with the Father, and always will be.
The Holy Spirit is not a Son, because he is not begotten, but he proceeds from the Father and from the Son alike, because he is the Will and Love of them both.
The Father always was, without beginning; and the Son always was with the Father, because he is the Father's Wisdom; the Holy Spirit always was, who is the Will and Love of them both.
The sun that shines over us is a bodily creature, and yet it has three properties in it: one is the bodily substance, that is, the sun's disc;

the second is the beam or brightness that always comes from the sun, which lights the whole world; the third is the heat, which comes to us with the beam. The beam is always from the sun, and always with it;
None of them is greater than another, nor any less than another; none is before another, nor any after another;
Each of the three is God, yet they are all one God, because they all have one nature, and one Godhead, and one substance, and one counsel,
Yet the Holy Spirit is not Christ's Father, and no Christian must ever believe that; rather, the Holy Spirit is the Will of the Father and of the Son;
nevertheless, the heating belongs to the heat, and the illumination belongs to the brightness.
But know that no one can speak fully about God, since we cannot even examine or explain the creatures that he created.
Or who can [grasp] all other things, since we cannot even fully take in with our sight the bodily things that we look at?
And yet it is a created thing, and it moves at God's direction. How much more, do you think, are God's presence, his might and his visitation everywhere?
Nothing stands against him, neither stone wall nor boarded wall, as they stand against the sun.
Nothing is hidden or unknown to him. You see a person's face, and God sees his heart. The Spirit of God searches the hearts of all people;
And those who believe in him and love him he cleanses and gladdens with his visitation, and the hearts of unbelieving men he passes by and shuns.
Let everyone also know that every person has three things in himself, inseparable and working together, just as God said when he first created man.
He said, "Let us make man in our likeness." And he then made Adam in his image. In what part does man have God's image in him? In the soul, not in the body.
A person's soul has in its nature the likeness of the Holy Trinity, because it has three things in it: memory, understanding, and will.
Through the memory a man thinks of the things that he has heard, or seen, or learned.
Through the understanding he understands all the things that he hears or sees. From the will come thoughts, and words, and deeds, both evil and good.

There is one soul, and one life, and one substance, which has these three things in it, working together inseparably; for where the memory is, there the understanding and the will are, and they are always together.
Yet none of these three is the soul itself. Rather, the soul remembers through the memory, understands through the understanding, and through the will it wills whatever pleases it;
And yet it is one soul and one life. So it has God's image in it, because it has three things in it working inseparably.
Yet the man is one man, and not a trinity. God truly, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, continues in a trinity of persons and in the unity of one Godhead.
Man does not exist as a trinity as God does, but he nevertheless has God's image in his soul through the three things that we spoke of before.
There was a heretic called Arius, who contended against a bishop named Alexander, a wise man of right belief.
Then the heretic said that Christ, the Son of God, could not be equal to his Father, nor as mighty as he;
and he said that the Father existed before the Son, and took his example from men, how every son in this life is younger than the father.
Then the holy bishop Alexander said in reply to him, "God always was, and his Wisdom was always begotten of him, and that Wisdom is his Son, just as mighty as the Father."
Then the heretic obtained the emperor's support for his heresy, and called a council against the bishop, and meant to turn all the people to his heresies.
Then the bishop kept vigil one night in God's church, and called to his Lord, and said this: "Almighty God, judge a just judgment between me and Arius."
The next morning they came to the council. Then the heretic said to his companions that he wanted to go out to relieve himself.
When he came to the privy and sat down, all his entrails came out of him at the seat, and he sat there dead.
Then God showed that he was as emptied in his bowels as he had already been in his faith.
He wanted to make Christ less than he is, and to diminish the honour of his Godhead; so he was given as shameful a death as he well deserved.
There was another heretic who was called Sabellius. He said that the Father was the Father when he wished, and again, when he wished, he was the Son;
and again, when he wished, he would be the Holy Ghost; and so he would be one God. Then this heretic also perished along with his heresy.
Now again, the Jewish people, who killed Christ as he himself willed and allowed, say that they will believe in the Father, but not in the Son, whom their kinsmen killed.
Their faith is nothing, and so they perish. For our redemption Christ allowed them to kill him. All mankind could not have done it if he himself had not been willing;
but the Holy Father created and made mankind through his Son, and he wished afterwards to redeem us through that same Son from the torment of hell, when we were condemned.
He could have had us without any suffering, but that seemed unjust to him.
We hold the faith that Christ himself taught his apostles, and that they taught to all mankind; and God has confirmed and established that faith with many miracles.
We must believe that every person's soul is created by God, yet it is not of God's own nature.
The soul does not exist anywhere beforehand. Instead, God creates it at that very moment and places it in the body, and lets it have its own free choice, whether to sin or to avoid sins.
Yet it always needs God's help so that it can avoid sins and come back to its Creator through good merits, because without God no one does anything good.
We must also believe that every body that has received a soul will rise on Judgement Day with the same body that it has now, and will receive the reward for all its deeds:
